title: What if you threw a baseball at nearly light speed?

A_identity.core_topic: What physically happens when a baseball is pitched at 90% of light speed.
A_identity.audience_inferred: Curious general viewers who enjoy science taken to comic extremes; inferred from text only.
A_identity.primary_question: What would happen if you tried to hit a baseball pitched at 0.9c?
A_identity.promise: A nanosecond-by-nanosecond account of the disaster, flagged in advance as ending badly.
A_identity.style: Deadpan, precise, present-tense narration with dry asides.
A_identity.pov: First-person narrator ('my best guess') shifting to second person for the hilltop observer.

B_hook.opening_quote: What would happen if you tried to hit a baseball pitched at 90% the speed of light?
B_hook.construction: Reader question read verbatim, one assumption to remove the 'how' objection, then a deadpan verdict that it ends badly before any explanation.
B_hook.first_curiosity_trigger: The verdict that many things happen very quickly and it does not end well for batter or pitcher.
B_hook.conflict_or_contradiction: A normal, everyday pitch is paired with relativistic speed; 'normal physics' is promised to produce abnormal results.
B_hook.withheld: What exactly goes wrong, how badly, and how far the damage spreads.
B_hook.audience_expectation: A step-by-step destruction sequence with real physics behind it.
B_hook.promise_strength_reason: The outcome direction is stated and a specific format (nanosecond portrait) is promised, so the viewer knows what they are waiting for.
B_hook.opening_to_payoff: The doom verdict is paid off by the batter being carried through the backstop and then by the city-scale blast.
B_hook.why_may_hold: The verdict plausibly converts 'what happens?' into 'how bad does it get?', which each later step can escalate.
B_hook.weaknesses: The assumption-setting sentences delay the first concrete image by a few lines.

K_assessment.distinctive_technique: Narrating a catastrophe in the calm procedural voice of a rulebook, then literally citing the rulebook.
K_assessment.biggest_risk: Dense physics vocabulary in the middle may lose viewers unfamiliar with fusion or plasma.
K_assessment.lesson: Take the question's frame seriously to the very end; the last answer can come from the frame rather than the science.

L_formula: Grant one magical assumption and declare normal physics from there.
Give a flat verdict that it ends badly and promise a time-sliced account.
Explain the single physical fact that breaks intuition (air cannot move aside).
Chain consequences in order, each with a time marker.
Show the asker's implied scenario is impossible (batter never sees it).
Reset to a distant human observer to show the full scale.
Close by applying an official rule from the question's own domain.

lenses.architect: Two-act build: a nanosecond close-up followed by a seconds-long wide shot, joined by a viewpoint reset.
lenses.surgeon: 'Unfortunately' and 'It does, however' are the hinge words that turn description into consequence.
lenses.viral: The rule-citation closing line is the most quotable because it compresses the whole joke into one bureaucratic sentence.
lenses.critic: The hook spends several sentences on ground rules before any image; the title has to carry attention until then.
lenses.curiosity: Curiosity is sustained by 'how bad' rather than 'what', since the verdict is given early.
lenses.platform: The opening sentence is itself a natural-language search query; the hilltop passage could stand alone as a short segment.
lenses.integrator: Physics, humour and structure share one device: procedural calm applied to escalating destruction.
lenses.tradeoffs: Giving the verdict early sacrifices surprise about the outcome in exchange for anticipation about the mechanism.
